thread.title: When the Momentum Starts to Fade

author: Avi Salzman
title: When the Momentum Starts to Fade
text:
Photo: Randen Pederson By Avi Salzman June 30, 2018 Vital Signs
A quarter full of twists, turns, and tariffs had one more swerve at the end.
Stocks ended the second quarter on a sour note, as the major indexes went south in the last few minutes of trading on Friday. The Dow had traded 293 points higher earlier in the day, led by Nike (NKE), whose strong earnings sent the stock up 11%. But the mood suddenly turned after 3 p.m., as end-of-quarter selling pressure picked up. The Dow closed up 55 points.
A $3.4 billion sell order that was entered toward the end of the day typified the mood, says Christopher Harvey, head of equity strategy at Wells Fargo Securities.
“Just before trading closed on Friday, things accelerated as people took off exposure,” he says.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the week down 309 points, or 1.3%, to close at 24,271.41. The S&P 500 fell 37 points, or 1.3%, to 2718.37, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 183 points, or 2.4%, to 7510.30.
Large-cap fundamental fund managers had been beating the market by 2.45 percentage points as of June 20, but a drop in price for momentum stocks over the past week erased some of those gains. Given that June 30 is one of the key dates that managers are judged on, they started to get more defensive to preserve their earlier gains, Harvey says. “Momentum has performed well over the last two years,” he says “It was a bit stretched. Once something stops working, there’s an incentive for people to start locking in profits.”
Investors pulled $29.3 billion from U.S. stock funds and exchange-traded funds in the week ended June 27, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch. It was the largest such outflow since February. The vast majority of that money went into money-market funds.
Even if the last note was off-key, the rest of the quarter was more harmonious.
For the quarter, all three major indexes were higher – by just 0.7% for the Dow but 2.9% for the S&P 500 and 6.3% for the Nasdaq. It was again a strong quarter for technology stocks, with Apple (AAPL) rising 10.3% and Facebook (FB) closing near all-time highs.
Small-caps also prospered during the quarter, with the Russell 2000 surging 7.4%.
Macro trends have favored smaller companies. The dollar rose 5.5% in the quarter against the euro, hurting larger companies that export more goods. And smaller companies are less likely to be hurt by a trade war, because they sell more of their products domestically.
Trade war headlines didn’t help the market on Friday—or for most of the week. General Motors (GM) warned the Trump administration that tariffs on cars and parts could force the company to add thousands of dollars to the price of its vehicles and reduce demand. Earlier in the week, Harley-Davidson (HOG) said the European tariffs levied in response to U.S. duties would hurt its margins and force it to move some production overseas.
Nonetheless, some fund managers headed into the quarter-end feeling optimistic. The tariffs are still dwarfed by the tax cuts, whose full positive effects haven’t made their way to the market, argues David Waddell, chief investment strategist at Memphis-based Waddell & Associates. “I don’t think people have really done the math on the tax cuts,” he says.
Waddell has been positioning for a resurgence in value stocks, which have continued to trail growth names this year. He took notice of Friday’s shift toward a more defensive trading posture.
“It’s time for traders to recalibrate,” he says. “We’re in the last day of the quarter, so I don’t want to read too much into the rotation because it may just be rebalancing. But if you want to go into the next quarter with your contrarian hat on, you want to own emerging markets, you want to own value stocks. The contrarians are making the bets today.”
